title: Carbon-A: Finding genes in known and unknown genomes
gist: Hugging Face's bio team releases Carbon-A, a 1.2B-parameter DNA model that predicts protein-coding regions across eukaryotes (F1 0.944 on 42 genomes), and the Carbon Annotation Database with 566 million predicted loci across 22,617 taxa. It frames open bio models as a hedge against dependence on closed frontier labs, and expects 2027 to be the year of bio.

insights.claim: Hugging Face's bio team believes major AI labs are gearing up to tackle biology as the next frontier after cyber and math, and expects 2027 to be the year for bio.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Signals where open-source AI labs expect the next capability and funding push.
insights.quote: We think 2027 will be the year for bio.
insights.locator: Why working on models for biology now?

insights.claim: The authors argue open bio models are needed so researchers do not depend on the priorities and policies of a handful of closed labs, citing a controversy over Claude refusing legitimate biology questions.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Closed-model refusals and policy are an adoption driver for open scientific models.
insights.locator: But we’ve also seen how fragile the ecosystem can become

insights.claim: Sequencing cost and time have fallen by orders of magnitude, so genome assemblies are now generated far faster than they can be understood, moving the bottleneck to annotation.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Value is shifting from sequencing hardware to interpretation software and models.
insights.quote: We can now generate genome assemblies far faster than we can understand them.

insights.claim: Annotation still usually depends on transcript data, known proteins, interpolation from closely related species and expert involvement, all unevenly distributed across the tree of life.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Poorly studied species are underserved by current pipelines, creating room for a single general model.

insights.claim: Carbon-A is a 1.2B-parameter model that predicts protein-coding regions directly from DNA with one model across mammals, vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi and protists, using a 98,304-base-pair context window with nucleotide-resolution predictions on both strands.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: A single shared model replaces clade-specific gene finders.

insights.claim: Across 42 benchmark genomes Carbon-A reaches a macro-averaged nucleotide F1 of 0.944 and beats AUGUSTUS, Helixer, Tiberius, ANNEVO, OrionGeno, SegmentNT and NTv3 at nucleotide, exon and gene level.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Self-reported benchmark lead over established gene finders and DNA foundation models.

insights.claim: Carbon-A scores better against a 2026 pig assembly than the 2017 assembly in its training snapshot, which the authors read as evidence that it learned coding regularities rather than memorizing noisy RefSeq labels.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Robustness to label noise suggests the model can improve as references improve.

insights.claim: An animal-only Carbon-A checkpoint annotates unseen plant genomes well, and on Tetrahymena thermophila, which uses a nonstandard genetic code, it reaches 0.960 nucleotide F1 without a species-specific model.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Out-of-distribution transfer supports the claim of learning generalizable coding features.
insights.locator: One model across the tree of life

insights.claim: The released model outputs a per-gene confidence score with AUROC 0.876 for separating exact CDS matches from other predictions, letting users trade coverage for precision.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Usable confidence scores make the database filterable for different risk tolerances.

insights.claim: Iso-Seq data from cat, Syrian hamster, chicken and Arabidopsis support several Carbon-A coding regions absent from RefSeq, suggesting some disagreements with the reference reflect missing annotations rather than model errors.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Early independent evidence that the model finds real genes, though limited to four species.

insights.claim: Carbon-A reaches roughly 0.62 complete-CDS support in Iso-Seq data, close to the reference and above all other ab initio systems tested.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Matches the curated reference level without using transcript data.

insights.claim: Iso-Seq shows predicted regions are transcribed but does not establish they are translated into proteins or what they do; next steps are ribosome profiling and mass spectrometry.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Candidate genes remain hypotheses until proteomic and functional evidence arrives.
insights.quote: They do not yet establish that those RNAs are translated into proteins—or what those proteins do.

insights.claim: The Carbon Annotation Database currently covers 48,167 GenBank assemblies from 22,617 taxa, around 27 trillion base pairs and 566 million predicted protein-coding loci, about 11.0x more taxa and 9.0x more sequence than the RefSeq training corpus.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Scale of public annotation expands by an order of magnitude over curated references.

insights.claim: Roughly half of the target GenBank genomes are annotated, another batch is planned in three weeks, and the annotations will soon be available through EMBL; each prediction links to coordinates, coding sequence, protein and confidence score.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Institutional distribution via EMBL would raise the dataset's credibility and reach.
insights.locator: We have now annotated roughly half

insights.claim: Fergal Martin of EMBL-EBI said the dataset, built on public genomes in the European Nucleotide Archive, could help researchers interpret and compare genes and genomes at scale.
insights.speaker: Fergal Martin
insights.so_what: An external institutional endorsement of the approach.

insights.claim: The decoder still produces a single consensus path per locus; explicit multi-isoform prediction is one of the clearest next steps, alongside proteomics validation and database expansion.
insights.speaker: Georgia Channing
insights.so_what: Isoform handling is the main stated modeling gap.
insights.locator: The current model already shows signals
